newsitem.title: USA: UPS strike hits 21pct NY buyers - BoT-Mitsub.
newsitem.headline: UPS strike hits 21pct NY buyers - BoT-Mitsub.

text.p: The United Parcel Service strike is causing severe problems for nearly 21 percent of New York area purchasing executives, a National Association of Purchasing Management-New York survey conducted by Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi Ltd showed.

Conducted over the last two days, the "Special Snapshot Survey" showed that 4.2 percent of respondents reported "very severe" disruptions in purchasing and deliveries, with 16.7 percent saying the strike caused "severe" problems. Rounding out the poll on this question, an even 50 percent saw a "moderate" impact and 29.2 percent viewed it as "slight."
While about 80 percent of respondents felt the strike impact was moderate to slight so far, many saw the potential for increased impact if the strike continues.

"Other carriers can't sustain their current level of operation for an extended period," one purchasing manager said, adding that the "first few days weren't too bad, but the strike is now starting to take its toll."
There may be "potential strikes at other carriers as contracts become due," another respondent said.

The strike has contributed to inventory problems, with 8.3 percent of the purchasing managers reporting "too much" inventory, 29.2 percent experiencing "shortages" and the remaining 62.5 percent seeing "no problems" at this time.

"Since manufacturing activity is a relatively small portion of local-area business activity, this finding more heavily reflected the service-sector base of the New York region, which tends to be more of a user than supplier of goods," Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi said.

The need to find alternative package carriers is increasing shipping costs for most with 66.7 percent of the New York managers polled reporting "higher" costs and the other 33.3 percent seeing no change since the strike began.

The exact same distribution was seen on the question of aggregate supplier delivery time, with 66.7 percent reporting it as "slower" and the remaining 33.3 percent experiencing "on time" delivery. If slower, the average delay was two to three days, according to the median response.
All percentages may not total 100 percent due to rounding.
